assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics extend the second law and thermodynamic bookkeeping to small, driven, far-from-equilibrium systems with exact, universal relations. This is the kind of simple, general mechanism that organises a very wide range of phenomena, from molecular motors and single-molecule pulling to colloids and nanodevices. The results are clean, rigorously derived and conceptually original.
assessment.attribution: Evans and collaborators (with Gallavotti-Cohen in the background) identified the fluctuation relation, Jarzynski the nonequilibrium work equality, Crooks the detailed fluctuation theorem, and Seifert the consistent trajectory-level framework of stochastic thermodynamics. Four credited names exceed the three-laureate limit. I would favour Jarzynski, Evans and Seifert as the broadest conceptual coverage, but Crooks's contribution is decisive for the experimental use and the split is genuinely contestable. Others outside the credited list (Gallavotti, Cohen, Bustamante and the single-molecule experimentalists) also have claims.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The theorems have been tested repeatedly in single-molecule, colloidal and electronic experiments over more than two decades, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee regards this as physics-prize-level impact on measured phenomena rather than a formal theoretical framework.
Credit is spread over more than three people and over the experimentalists who validated it; any three-person split omits a decisive contributor.
I am relying on my own recollection of the chronology (Evans-Cohen-Morriss 1993, Jarzynski 1997, Crooks 1999, Seifert 2005) and have not verified it independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase established that gauge potentials and geometry have direct physical consequences, and the geometric-phase idea is a strikingly simple, universal mechanism. It recurs in molecular physics, optics, condensed matter (Berry curvature, anomalous Hall, topological bands) and wave physics in general. Few single concepts have travelled so far across disciplines.
assessment.attribution: Two names are credited and map cleanly to the two ideas: Aharonov (with Bohm, who is not in the credited list and is deceased) for the topological phase effect, and Berry for the general adiabatic geometric phase. Pancharatnam, Ehrenberg-Siday and Bohm have historical claims, and the Aharonov-Bohm part is not a single-laureate story without Bohm. A prize framed on Berry's phase with Aharonov is workable but the priority narrative is not fully tidy.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of independent experimental confirmation (electron interferometry, mesoscopic rings, optical and molecular geometric phases). The risk is not prematurity but that the work is old and the committee may judge its moment to have passed.
uncertainties: Bohm's absence and the Ehrenberg-Siday and Pancharatnam precedents complicate a clean priority claim.
The two effects may be seen as separate discoveries combined for convenience.
Whether the committee still considers the idea unrewarded in practice, given how much of it has been absorbed into topological matter prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect opened a field of symmetry-protected topological matter. The Kane-Mele proposal is a clean theoretical idea, and the HgTe observation of edge transport made it a physical reality. The conceptual reach (topology of band structure, protected boundary states) is large and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele are the central theorists on the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification, and Molenkamp's group delivered the experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells. The supplied credit omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (who proposed HgTe) and the three-dimensional topological insulator contributors (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan, Hsieh), so the allocation is genuinely unresolved. The Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio is defensible but not obviously unique.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The experimental and theoretical picture has been confirmed in many materials over fifteen-plus years. The HgTe result is robust though the quantisation is imperfect in practice.
uncertainties: The prize-worthy discovery has several plausible laureate sets, and the one here excludes key theorists such as Bernevig and Zhang, who is deceased.
Overlap with the related candidate on topological insulators and quantum anomalous Hall means the committee should not reward the same underlying discovery twice.
My fit to this area is as a neighbour (theory and statistical physics), not a specialist in topological band theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type many-body models with tunable parameters, giving a controlled way to test statistical-physics ideas such as the Mott transition, quantum phase transitions and out-of-equilibrium dynamics. The programme joins clean model Hamiltonians to precise experiments, which I value highly. The proposal-plus-observation pairing (Jaksch-Zoller, Greiner) is a model for theory-experiment interplay.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Cirac supplied the proposals, Greiner and Bloch the decisive experimental demonstrations (Mott-insulator transition, quantum gas microscopes), and Dalibard has strong credit for cold-atom techniques and synthetic gauge fields. Five credited names must be cut to three. I favour Zoller for theory with Bloch and Greiner for experiment, but Cirac's and Dalibard's claims are real and the overlap with the trapped-ion and Rydberg candidates blurs the boundaries.
assessment.maturity: Largely mature for the lattice quantum-simulation core, since the techniques are widely replicated. The aspiration of solving open problems (e.g. Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram) is still in progress, so impact on unsolved questions is not yet fully demonstrated.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with Bose-Einstein condensation (already recognised) and with other quantum-simulation and quantum-computing candidates.
Whether simulation results have yet answered a question that analytical theory could not.
Too many credited people for a three-laureate prize, with unresolved allocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Flocking theory shows that long-range order can exist in two-dimensional nonequilibrium systems with continuous symmetry, evading the Mermin-Wagner theorem, through a minimal model (Vicsek) and a hydrodynamic theory (Toner-Tu). It is a textbook example of a universal mechanism in a messy many-body system, and it founded the active-matter field. I find the conceptual originality high.
assessment.attribution: Vicsek introduced the minimal model of self-propelled alignment, and Toner and Tu derived the hydrodynamic theory and the scaling exponents and the order in two dimensions. The three credited names map onto these contributions plainly. Credit for the experimental side (bacteria, colloids, bird flocks) is diffuse and no individual is clearly decisive.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The theory and numerical simulations are well established and many experiments on active systems support the qualitative picture, but quantitative tests of the exact Toner-Tu exponents in clean experimental systems remain limited.
uncertainties: Quantitative experimental verification of the predicted scaling exponents is incomplete.
Some committee members may regard active matter as insufficiently established or too far from fundamental physics for the prize.
I may overweight this because it lies close to my own research interests in stochastic and nonequilibrium theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Energy-landscape theory explains how a heteropolymer finds its native structure on biological timescales by borrowing the statistical mechanics of disordered systems (spin-glass ideas, the principle of minimal frustration, funnels). It resolves Levinthal's paradox conceptually and gives an organising principle for a core biophysical problem. This is statistical physics at its best, though the prize has already honoured protein structure prediction in chemistry.
assessment.attribution: Bryngelson and Wolynes (1987) introduced the spin-glass-inspired picture, Wolynes and Onuchic developed the funnel landscape, and Dill contributed lattice models and the hydrophobic-collapse view. Bryngelson and others outside the credited list also have strong claims. The three-name set is plausible but Dill's role is distinct in character and the split is not obviously uniquely right.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a conceptual framework and supported by simulation and experiment (folding kinetics, coarse-grained models). Its status as a physics discovery rather than a modelling paradigm is arguable, and it is entangled with the chemistry community's recognition.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as physics or as chemistry and biology, given the 2024 chemistry award on protein structure.
Experimental tests are indirect and the framework is partly interpretive.
Attribution between Wolynes, Onuchic, Dill, Bryngelson and other early contributors is disputed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is an exact solution in infinite dimensions that supplies a controlled, non-perturbative description of strongly correlated electrons, including the Mott transition. It is a method with a clear physical idea (local self-energy mapped to an impurity problem) and wide use in quantum materials. It is analogous to mean-field theory in statistical mechanics, which appeals to my training.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimensional limit, Georges and Kotliar established the mapping to a self-consistent impurity problem, and Georges, Kotliar, Krauth and Rozenberg developed the full theory. The three credited names are the natural core, but the omission of Metzner, Krauth and Rozenberg leaves the priority picture contestable.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a method, widely adopted and extended (DMFT+DFT, cluster extensions). Its predictive success for specific real materials is mixed, and the case for a prize rests more on conceptual and methodological impact than on a single confirmed discovery.
uncertainties: A method rather than an experimentally confirmed discovery, which some members may weigh against it.
Credit is spread over several theorists beyond the three listed.
Quantitative predictive success for real correlated materials is uneven.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The KTHNY theory of two-dimensional melting, with defect unbinding in two stages and an intermediate hexatic phase, is a elegant example of a universal, defect-driven mechanism for a phase transition. It extends the Kosterlitz-Thouless ideas to a physical class of systems, and has been tested in colloids and other 2D systems. It is conceptually clean and exemplifies the kind of simple mechanism I value.
assessment.attribution: Nelson and Halperin, and independently Young, developed the theory of dislocation-mediated melting building on Kosterlitz and Thouless, whose topological-defect work was recognised in 2016. This candidate is therefore a continuation, and the novelty relative to the 2016 prize is part of the question. Credit assignment among the three names is reasonably clear, but Kosterlitz and Thouless sit outside the list.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Colloidal and simulation experiments have confirmed two-step melting and the hexatic phase in several systems, though the nature of the transitions (first order vs continuous) is system dependent.
uncertainties: Substantial conceptual overlap with the 2016 prize may make the committee reluctant.
Experimental and numerical evidence shows system-dependent behaviour (first-order melting in some systems), so the universal picture is not fully uniform.
Halperin also appears on another candidate, which would need to be handled if both advanced.
